question.body: According to paragraph 1, what do smartphone notifications do to the people in the room?

options.text: Repeatedly draw their attention away from conversations
Help them listen more closely to others
Make their time pass more slowly
Prevent them from looking at screens

question.explanation: Paragraph 1 expressly describes notifications interrupting conversations and attracting attention to screens. A: Directly restates both effects in the passage. B: Closer listening contradicts interrupted conversations. C: No slowing of time is claimed. D: Attention is drawn towards screens, not prevented from reaching them.
question.passage_text:
(1) A room is filled with people whose faces glow in the light of their smartphones. Moments drift away like autumn leaves in the wind. Notifications repeatedly interrupt conversations and draw fingers towards screens.

(2) When phones are out of reach, people feel anxious and incomplete. The writer compares this feeling to a phantom limb: an absent digital device seems like a missing part of oneself. Fear of missing out drives repeated checking.

(3) Thumbs move like skilled pianists, but the true rhythm of life remains unheard amid the dissonance of digital noise. Constant connectivity creates a hunch on shoulders, a physical sign of the burden of information overload. Minds stay alert for the next like, share or comment.

(4) Despite efforts to stay connected, people become increasingly isolated among digital faces. Genuine connections are fleeting amid the constant clamour for attention. The search for digital validation sacrifices meaningful moments and shared experiences.

(5) The writer urges readers to value presence and engagement in moments that matter. What defines people is the depth of their connections and the richness of their experiences, rather than their number of likes or followers.

question.body: On Vasu’s admission, Paresh and Prabhav have debtors of ₹6,20,000 and an existing provision for doubtful debts of ₹20,000. Debtors worth ₹15,000 have turned bad and must be written off. Which entries correctly record this write-off?

options.text: Bad Debts A/c Dr ₹15,000; To Debtors A/c ₹15,000. Then Provision for Doubtful Debts A/c Dr ₹15,000; To Bad Debts A/c ₹15,000.
Bad Debts A/c Dr ₹15,000; To Debtors A/c ₹15,000. Then Revaluation A/c Dr ₹15,000; To Provision for Doubtful Debts A/c ₹15,000.
Revaluation A/c Dr ₹15,000; To Debtors A/c ₹15,000.
Bad Debts A/c Dr ₹15,000; To Revaluation A/c ₹15,000.

question.explanation: The existing 20000 provision covers the 15000 write-off. Debit Bad Debts and credit Debtors; then debit the provision and credit Bad Debts. Remaining provision is 5000 and net debtor value stays 600000; no new revaluation loss is invented. A: Matches the write-off and its adjustment against the existing provision. B: Creates or increases a provision through Revaluation instead of consuming the existing provision. C: Charges a new revaluation loss while leaving the covering provision unadjusted. D: Does not credit debtors and improperly credits Revaluation.
